title: Writing Character & Dialogue
keyIdea: Dialogue lets readers hear characters and see who they are. Put the exact spoken words inside speech marks, with the comma, question mark or exclamation mark inside the closing mark. Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes. Use said, or an action beat that shows the feeling, rather than adverbs that tell it. Give each character a voice of their own. End the story by reflecting on what the events meant, not just on the last thing that happened.
familyTip: Read a page of dialogue from a novel your child likes. Cover the tags and see if you can still tell who is speaking, then talk about how. Next, write a short argument between two very different people together, taking one character each, and set it out with speech marks and new lines.

visual.caption: Does the line show the feeling, or just tell it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: punctuate speech, give each speaker a new line, use action beats, hear each voice and end with reflection.

kid: Dialogue is what your characters say out loud. Put their exact words inside speech marks. The comma or question mark goes inside the closing mark: “Don’t open it,” Mia whispered. The tag, like Mia whispered, starts with a small letter because the sentence is not over.
Start a new line each time a new person speaks. That is how the reader keeps track of who is talking. A character’s actions stay in the same paragraph as their own words.

Show feelings, do not just name them. “I’m fine,” Gran said nervously tells us. “I’m fine.” Gran’s cup rattled on its saucer shows us. Said is a good tag because readers hardly notice it. An action beat can replace the tag and show who is speaking.

Give each character their own voice. A blunt person uses short words. A formal person uses long, polite sentences. Open with a hook that sets the scene and the point of view. End by looking back at what the events meant or how a character changed. That is stronger than a twist or a dream.
adult: Ages 11 to 14. This matches CCSS W.6.3 to W.8.3: write narratives that set up context and point of view, develop characters through dialogue, pacing and description, and end with a conclusion that reflects on events. It also matches the KS3 English writing aim to write imaginative stories with effective dialogue. Key terms: dialogue, speech marks (inverted commas), reporting clause or tag, action beat, voice, characterisation, reflective conclusion.

The conventions are fixed. Spoken words go inside inverted commas. Punctuation that belongs to the speech goes inside the closing mark. A comma replaces the full stop when a reporting clause follows. Each new speaker starts a new paragraph. Writers on craft, such as Browne and King, advise using said or an action beat, and letting the words and actions carry the emotion.

Common mistakes: a full stop before the tag (“Wait here.” said Mum); the comma outside the closing mark; one paragraph for a whole conversation; a fancy tag or an adverb on every line; characters who all sound alike; dialogue that only repeats what the narrator said; and endings that stop at the last action, or cancel the story with a dream. Be careful that a ‘reflective’ ending reflects on these events, not a general moral bolted on.

In the lab your child fills six punctuation gaps in two lines of speech, splits a block of dialogue into paragraphs, chooses action beats over adverbs three times, sorts six lines between a blunt and a formal speaker by voice alone, and picks the two endings that reflect.

choices: “Close the door,” said Dad.
“Close the door.” said Dad.
“Close the door”, said Dad.
practice.hint: The sentence goes on after the speech, and the punctuation sits next to the spoken words.
practice.explain: A comma, not a full stop, comes before a tag like said Dad, and it goes inside the closing speech mark.

practice.prompt: Two characters take turns to speak. There are {n} lines of speech, and the speaker changes every time. How many paragraphs does the dialogue need?
practice.hint: Each change of speaker starts a new paragraph.
practice.explain: The speaker changes on every line, so each of the {n} lines gets its own paragraph.

practice.prompt: Which line best shows that Ana is nervous?
choices: Ana twisted her sleeve. “Is it my turn?”
“Is it my turn?” Ana asked nervously.
“I am very nervous,” said Ana.
practice.hint: Which line lets you see the feeling instead of being told it?
practice.explain: Twisting her sleeve is an action beat that shows nerves. The other two name the feeling.

practice.prompt: A scene has {a} lines by Kez and {b} lines by Mr Ashby. They take turns, so each line is a new speaker. How many paragraphs is that?
practice.hint: Count every line, because each one is a change of speaker.
practice.explain: {a} lines and {b} lines make {=a+b} turns, so {=a+b} paragraphs.

practice.prompt: Which ending reflects on the story?
choices: I still think about that night, and how Gran trusted me with the truth.
Then we went home. The end.
Suddenly I woke up. It was all a dream.
practice.hint: Which one looks back on what the events meant?
practice.explain: The first ending looks back and shows what changed for the narrator. The others stop the action or cancel the story.

pool.prompt: Where does the question mark go? “Are you coming_” asked Sam_
choices: Inside the closing speech mark, then a full stop after Sam
After the word Sam, at the end
Outside the closing speech mark
pool.hint: The question belongs to the spoken words.
pool.explain: It reads “Are you coming?” asked Sam. The question mark is part of the speech, so it goes inside the marks.

pool.prompt: In a conversation, when should you start a new paragraph?
choices: Each time the speaker changes
Only when the scene changes
After every sentence
pool.hint: How does a reader keep track of who is talking?
pool.explain: A new speaker means a new paragraph. One speaker’s words and actions stay together.

pool.prompt: Which tag is usually the best choice for plain speech?
choices: said
chortled
exclaimed loudly
pool.hint: Which word lets the reader focus on the spoken words?
pool.explain: Said is almost invisible to readers, so the speech itself does the work. Fancy tags and adverbs pull attention away.

pool.prompt: Who is more likely to say “Nope. Not happening.”?
choices: A blunt, impatient teenager
A formal, polite headteacher
You cannot tell from the words
pool.hint: Look at the length of the sentences and the word choice.
pool.explain: Short, clipped words and no politeness fit a blunt character. Voice shows who is speaking.

pool.prompt: A conversation has {n} turns. Each turn needs an opening and a closing speech mark. How many speech marks is that?
pool.hint: Every turn has one opening mark and one closing mark.
pool.explain: {n} turns with 2 marks each is {=2*n} speech marks.

pool.prompt: What does an action beat do?
choices: Shows a feeling and who is speaking through an action
Names the feeling with an adverb
Ends the conversation
pool.hint: Think of Gran’s cup rattling on its saucer.
pool.explain: An action like a rattling cup shows Gran is nervous and tells us she is the one speaking, without an adverb.

pool.prompt: Which opening sets up the setting and point of view with a hook?
choices: The attic smelled of dust, and I knew I shouldn’t be up there.
This is a story about a diary.
Once there was a boy. He was called Leo.
pool.hint: Which one puts you in a place, inside a narrator’s head, with a question in your mind?
pool.explain: It gives a setting (the attic), a first-person point of view (I) and a hook (why shouldn’t they be there?).

pool.prompt: Why is “It was all a dream” a weak ending?
choices: It cancels everything that happened, so nothing matters
Dreams cannot be written about
It is too short to be an ending
pool.hint: What happens to the events of the story if none of them were real?
pool.explain: A dream ending wipes out the events, so the reader feels cheated. A reflective ending shows what they meant.

pool.prompt: Your scene has {a} lines of dialogue. {b} of them only repeat what the narrator already said, so you cut them. How many lines are left?
pool.hint: Take away the lines that do no new work.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} leaves {=a-b} lines. Every line left now shows character or moves the plot.
